section_summary: This section follows the prosecution, conviction, imprisonment and prospective release of Yukichi George Ozawa, a Japanese national publicly suspected of espionage but convicted only of practicing medicine without a Cuban license. Later records report alleged Japanese intelligence activity around Cuba and Central America, including suspicious vessels, the movements of Ozawa and Kimura, and a visiting Japanese mission. The closing documents concern the distribution of Japanese propaganda in Cuba and Haiti, particularly material defending Japan’s actions in China.

subfiles.title: Trial of Yukichi George Ozawa
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, U.S. Embassy, Havana
subfiles.about: Transmits a Diario de la Marina report on the prosecution of Ozawa for practicing medicine without a license.
subfiles.summary: Matthews reports that the government attorney was seeking Ozawa’s conviction for unauthorized medical practice and that deportation was probable after any prison sentence. The attached April 16 clipping requests a sentence of one year and eight months and lists several of Ozawa’s aliases and alleged patients. The clipping also contains an unrelated report about the homicide prosecution of Juan Poey for killing Dolores Peñalver.

subfiles.title: Trial of Yukihi George Ozawa for alleged illegal practice of medicine
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, U.S. Embassy, Havana
subfiles.about: Reports testimony in Ozawa’s trial and encloses a detailed press account of the proceedings.
subfiles.summary: Ozawa claimed to possess a University of California medical degree and a New Jersey license, although neither had been produced, and falsely said that Ambassador Caffery had been his patient. The clipping describes his testimony, his defense counsel and previous attorneys, and Secret Police evidence concerning his possible espionage and naval connections. The police witness could not substantiate either the alleged theft of a U.S. Navy patent or service as a Japanese spy.

subfiles.title: Conviction of Yukichi George Ozawa for illegal practice of medicine
subfiles.doc_type: Embassy despatch with two newspaper clippings
subfiles.about: Reports Ozawa’s conviction and an initially reported sentence of one year and eight months.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports that Ozawa had been convicted of illegally practicing medicine and, according to the first press reports, sentenced to one year and eight months. El Mundo emphasized that espionage was not part of the court case. The Havana Post nevertheless repeated police claims that Ozawa had engaged in espionage and noted Israel Castellanos’s challenge to the authenticity of his medical documents.

subfiles.title: Ozawa sentenced to one year and one day of imprisonment
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, U.S. Embassy, Havana
subfiles.about: Corrects the previously reported length of Ozawa’s prison sentence.
subfiles.summary: Matthews reports that the officially announced sentence was one year and one day, rather than one year and eight months. The Diario de la Marina clipping lists patients whom Ozawa treated at the Anglo-American and Mazorra hospitals. It stresses that the court made no finding about espionage because no such charge had been brought.

subfiles.title: Impending Visit of Alleged Japanese Agent to Cuba
subfiles.from: M. W. Timberlake, U.S. Military Attaché
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Requests information about T. Makabayashi before his anticipated arrival in Cuba.
subfiles.summary: Makabayashi is described as the alleged head of a Japanese commercial and military intelligence system in Central America, then located in Limón, Costa Rica. The report says he traveled as a textile and machinery expert, sought the favor of Cuban agriculture secretary López Castro, and had allegedly encouraged labor trouble in Central America. A receipt stamp dates the filing to August 1938, but no clear document date survives in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch on suspected Japanese fishing craft
subfiles.about: Directs readers to a despatch concerning unidentified vessels near Cuba’s southern coast.
subfiles.summary: The note references despatch No. 1375 in file 837.628/17. It records a Cienfuegos report of unidentified fishing craft believed to be Japanese near the Zapata Swamp and mentions soundings between Cayo Largo and the Isle of Pines.

subfiles.title: Suspected Japanese vessels and soundings off southern Cuba
subfiles.from: J. Butler Wright, U.S. Embassy, Havana
subfiles.about: Reports rumors of Japanese fishing vessels and a vessel taking soundings off Cuba’s southern coast.
subfiles.summary: The vice consul at Cienfuegos relayed a Cuban naval commander’s report that unidentified craft believed Japanese had recently operated near the Zapata Swamp, an area thought capable of sheltering hostile aircraft or submarines. Wright treated the rumors cautiously but added A. Devere’s report that a vessel had taken soundings between Cienfuegos, Cayo Largo and the Isle of Pines. One crewman was reportedly Japanese and appeared not to be a regular fisherman.

subfiles.title: Yukihi George Ozawa
subfiles.from: Edward P. Lawton, U.S. Embassy, Havana
subfiles.about: Reports Ozawa’s impending release and Cuba’s inability to fund his deportation.
subfiles.summary: Lawton reports that Ozawa and about sixty other undesirable aliens would be released after serving their sentences because Cuba lacked funds for deportation. The Havana Post recaps Ozawa’s arrest, the unproven espionage suspicions, the Japanese minister’s denial that he was attached to the legation, and his conviction for unauthorized medical practice. It also names several other foreign prisoners expected to be released.

subfiles.title: Visit of special Japanese Mission to Cuba
subfiles.about: Cross-references a despatch and clipping about a visiting Japanese mission.
subfiles.summary: The note points to despatch No. 1658 and an El Mundo clipping on a special Japanese mission. The delegates were expected to reach Havana from Santo Domingo on February 7, remain until February 15, and then sail for Panama on a United Fruit Company vessel.

subfiles.title: Reported movements of George Ozawa and Kimura
subfiles.about: Relays a press correspondent’s report of Ozawa and another alleged Japanese spy traveling in eastern Cuba.
subfiles.summary: A Santiago de Cuba correspondent reported that an alleged spy called Dr. George Asa—believed by the Embassy to be George Ozawa—had been in Guantánamo during naval operations and later in Santiago de Cuba with Dominican revolutionists. He was reportedly seen in Camagüey with an alleged Japanese spy named Kimura on March 13. Ozawa was thought to have departed aboard the Norwegian ship Boreas for New York.

subfiles.title: Japanese propaganda distribution in Cuba
subfiles.about: Cross-references a despatch about intermediaries distributing Japanese propaganda in Cuba.
subfiles.summary: The note states that Japanese propaganda not sent directly to newspapers was distributed through Pedro Pablo Schmendt of North German Lloyd and Luis Clasing of the Hamburg-America Line. It directs readers to despatch No. 1864 in file 800.20210/264.

subfiles.title: Japanese propaganda in Cuba
subfiles.about: Cross-references comments on propaganda distributed by Japanese merchant Keitaro Chira.
subfiles.summary: The file note identifies Keitaro Chira, a Japanese merchant resident in Cuba, as a distributor of Japanese propaganda. It refers researchers to despatch No. 2228 in file 837.00-N/13 for the original document.

subfiles.title: Japanese Foreign Trade Association pamphlet in Haiti
subfiles.about: Comments on a Japanese pamphlet circulated in Haiti to defend Japan’s conduct in China.
subfiles.summary: Referring to Port-au-Prince despatch No. 30 of January 4, 1938, the memorandum notes that the Foreign Trade Association of Japan considered it necessary to justify Japan’s actions in China even in Haiti. The writer calls the arguments banal and concludes that the pamphlet sought to prevent political misunderstanding from harming trade between Japan and Haiti.
